items.name: Carrier USS George Washington Leaves Middle East After Three Months
items.summary: USS George Washington (CVN-73) left the Middle East after being on station for three months, a U.S. Pacific Fleet spokesperson confirmed Wednesday to USNI News.  George Washington is now in U.S. 7th Fleet. The spokesperson did not provide additional details, including which of George Washington’s escorts accompanied the ship. George Washington and its escorts USS Robert Smalls (CG-62) and destroyer USS Shoup (DDG-86) arrived in U.S. 5th Fleet on Aug. 19, USNI News previously reported. items.name: F-35C Lightning II Completes First Launch and Recovery Aboard a Gerald R. Ford-Class Aircraft Carrier
items.full_text:
PATUXENT RIVER, Md., Nov. 19, 2026– On the U.S. Navy’s birthday this year, Oct.13, Lockheed Martin’s F‑35C Lightning II marked a new chapter in naval aviation, completing its first recovery aboard the Gerald R. Ford-Class aircraft carrier PCU John F. Kennedy (CVN 79). The milestone connected the Navy’s 251-year legacy of innovation with the next generation of naval airpower.

Testing aboard the Kennedy marked the F‑35Cs’ first shipboard compatibility testing on the Navy’s newest aircraft carrier, demonstrating its ability to safely launch and recover from the new flight deck while generating critical data to support future carrier operations. Over 11 days of testing, two F‑35Cs from Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, completed 34 flights, 122 catapult launches and 122 arrested landings using the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) and Advanced Arresting Gear (AAG), both of which are the latest in technological advancements for carrier-based fixed-wing operations.

“This is a critical event for the F‑35C, Kennedy, and the United States Navy,” said Sean Jackson, vice president, Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Development Program. “For the first time, the aircraft has demonstrated launch and recovery operations from a Gerald R. Ford-Class flight deck, advancing the integration of fifth-generation fighter capability with the world’s most advanced carrier technology. With the completion of this test phase, the Navy has now cleared the F-35C for operations across its entire fleet of aircraft carriers.”

Ford‑class carriers introduce a fundamentally different operating environment, including:

Testing Delivers Critical Data

The effort followed shore-based trials conducted between January 2024 and May 2025. At sea, the integrated test team collected essential data to support:

Advancing 5th Generation Carrier Capability

This milestone confirms the F‑35C’s compatibility with and capability to operate from America’s next generation of carrier decks. Its stealth, advanced sensors and data-sharing capabilities provide a powerful foundation for future maritime and joint-force operations.

The F‑35C’s successful Ford‑Class testing moves the program closer to full operational integration aboard the fleet’s newest carriers.

items.name: F-35C completes first launch and recovery trials on a Ford-class carrier
items.summary: Two Navy F-35C Lightning II fighters have completed the jet’s first round of launch and recovery testing aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy.
items.full_text:
Two Navy F-35C Lightning II fighters have completed the jet’s first round of launch and recovery testing aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy, the Navy’s second Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier,Lockheed Martin said Thursday.

Over 11 days of testing that began Oct. 13, theNavy’s 251st birthday, the two jets made 34 flights and logged 122 catapult launches and 122 arrested landings, the company said. The aircraft belong to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23, or VX-23, known as the “Salty Dogs,” at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland.

The flights were part of Kennedy’s Aircraft Compatibility Testing, which assesses how the ship’s launch and recovery equipment works with Navy aircraft, according to the Navy. The first arrested landing came onOct. 13, and the first catapult launch onOct. 14, Navy photo captions show.

Unlike Nimitz-class carriers, which launch and recover aircraft with steam catapults and hydraulic arresting gear, Ford-class carriers use theElectromagnetic Aircraft Launch System, or EMALS, and theAdvanced Arresting Gear, or AAG. Lockheed said EMALS allows smoother, more precisely controlled launches, while AAG can handle a broader range of recovery conditions.

The Ford class also has a smaller island, the tower that houses the bridge and flight control, set about 140 feet farther back than on Nimitz-class ships. Lockheed said the island and a redesigned flight deck change airflow, exhaust patterns and deck operations.

The at-sea testing followed shore-based trials conducted from January 2024 to May 2025, the company said. It validated the jet’s structural models and verified the software and equipment behind EMALS and AAG. The data will help develop the launch and recovery guidance crews use on Ford-class ships.

“This is a critical event for the F-35C, Kennedy, and the United States Navy,” said Sean Jackson, vice president of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Development Program. “For the first time, the aircraft has demonstrated launch and recovery operations from a Gerald R. Ford-Class flight deck, advancing the integration of fifth-generation fighter capability with the world’s most advanced carrier technology.”

Jackson also said that upon completion of this test phase, “the Navy has now cleared the F-35C for operations across its entire fleet of aircraft carriers.”

“The ships are cleared to launch and recover F-35s once the launch and recovery bulletins are published,” a Lockheed official told Defense News. “They will not be ready to deploy until fully outfitted with supportingequipment.”

The Navy, the official added, has the “final clearance.”

The F-35Cfirst landed on a carrier in November 2014, aboard USS Nimitz off San Diego, and has since deployed from modified Nimitz-class carriers. The lead ship of the Ford class, USS Gerald R. Ford, has not deployed with the jet.

In 2019, a Navy spokesmantold USNI Newsthat both carrier classes could operate with F-35Cs by design but needed changes, such as more robust jet blast deflectors and classified spaces, for the jet to be more effective on a full-length deployment.Stars and Stripes reported in Octoberthat the Navy plans to retrofit the Ford to operate the F-35C.

Kennedy received those modifications during construction. In 2020, the Navychanged the ship’s construction contractto meet a legislative requirement that Kennedy be capable of deploying with the F-35C.

The Navy tookpreliminary acceptance of Kennedyon Sept. 29, after the ship completed acceptance trials in August. Preliminary acceptance allows the crew to test and train at sea while the shipbuilder finishes its work. The Navy said at the time that the ship was about 99% complete, and formal delivery is planned for spring 2027.

Michael Scanlon is a defense journalist covering air and space warfare. A former U.S. Air Force A-10 crew chief, he has supported land and sea programs for the U.S. Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.
